Abnormal ER-Golgi vesicular trafficking leads to podocyte detachment
abstract: Podocyte detachment represents a point of no return in the progression of proteinuric kidney diseases, yet the molecular mechanisms driving this process remain poorly understood. In this issue of Kidney International, Imai et al. report that suppression of N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor, a key regulator of endoplasmic reticulum-to-Golgi vesicular trafficking, contributes to impaired integrin maturation and podocyte detachment. These findings establish, for the first time, a critical role for endoplasmic reticulum-to-Golgi vesicular trafficking in maintaining podocyte integrity.

title: Estimating GFR: what it is, what it is not, and why prediction cannot settle the question
abstract: Schultheiss et al. show that replacing Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration with European Kidney Function Consortium cystatin C-based equations reclassifies women, but not men, into milder chronic kidney disease stages, while outcome prediction is unchanged. We argue that prediction of kidney failure cannot validate a glomerular filtration rate equation: dialysis initiation is a clinical decision, not a filtration measurement. The analysis is cross-sectional, leaving longitudinal performance untested. Equations are population tools; at the bedside, non-glomerular filtration rate determinants of both creatinine and cystatin C can mislead.

title: Fetal growth restriction and lifelong risk of acute kidney injury: advancing the developmental origins of kidney disease
abstract: Fetal growth restriction has long been associated with reduced nephron number and chronic kidney disease, but its relationship with acute kidney injury has remained unclear. Fog-Høyer et al. demonstrated that fetal growth restriction increases acute kidney injury risk from infancy through early adulthood, particularly in children with congenital anomalies. We examine the study's strengths, limitations, biological basis, and clinical relevance, highlighting opportunities for targeted risk stratification, preventive care, and future research.

title: Microvascular inflammation in kidney transplants: finally an effective treatment?
abstract: Microvascular inflammation-glomerulitis and peritubular capillaritis-is the hallmark histologic lesion of antibody-mediated allograft rejection and may also occur in the absence of donor-specific antibodies. In either case, microvascular inflammation leads to graft loss, and it has proven difficult to treat. As demonstrated in a study in this issue of Kidney International, targeting CD38, a glycoprotein expressed on both plasma cells and natural killer cells, shows great promise in treating microvascular inflammation in kidney transplants.

title: Kidney stone disease: to drink or not to drink—that is the question
abstract: Kidney stone prevention presents a paradox: an effective, safe, and inexpensive intervention-hydration-is widely recommended, yet difficult to implement in practice. The recent Prevention of Urinary Stones With Hydration (PUSH) trial by Desai et al. (n = 1658 patients) evaluated a behavioral strategy to increase fluid intake and reduce recurrence over 2 years but found no significant benefit compared with standard of care, despite modest increases in urinary volume. These results contrast with earlier trials, notably that of Borghi et al. in 1996, in which sustained urine output above 2 L/d significantly reduced stone recurrence. The limited efficacy of PUSH likely reflects insufficient adherence, with a minimal difference in urine output between active treatment and the control group, and improved baseline management in control subjects. Functional urinary symptoms and social constraints might have further hindered compliance. An important point to note is that these findings do not invalidate the protective role of increased urine volume but highlight the limitations of behavioral interventions alone. Effective prevention likely requires achieving a substantial increase in urine volume alongside comprehensive dietary and pharmacologic management.

title: The macrophage paradox in renal AL amyloidosis: lessons from histology and imaging
abstract: In renal amyloid light chain amyloidosis, sustained and deep hematologic response drives organ response that continues to improve over time. Rauf et al. demonstrate that macrophage infiltration in kidney biopsies portends progression to renal replacement therapy despite hematologic response, whereas amyloid regression on serum amyloid P component scintigraphy independently predicts favorable outcomes. These findings offer insights into the mechanisms of renal involvement and highlight the complex, context-dependent role of macrophages in amyloid clearance and tissue injury.

Unfortunately, in this old version of Supplementary Table S1, owing to an unintended mishap during the compilation of the Supplementary Table S1, the columns containing patients’ pathological grading/isotypes information and the chronic kidney disease G-staging data were inadvertently merged, which led to display anomalies and an error in the affected Supplementary Table S1.

title: Fingerprinting the polycystic kidney: radiomics of the noncystic parenchyma for earlier ADPKD detection
abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease risk stratification relies on total kidney volume, a validated marker of cyst burden and progression. Kremer et al.'s pilot study used rapid breath-hold magnetic resonance fingerprinting with radiomics to evaluate noncystic renal parenchyma in children and young adults. Quantitative T1/T2 texture features distinguished autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease from controls independently of total kidney volume, cyst fraction, age, or body size, suggesting early tissue changes. Small, cross-sectional, unmatched data require longitudinal validation of reproducibility, prognostic value, and clinical utility.

title: Are we ready for the widespread application of transcutaneous measurement of the glomerular filtration rate?
abstract: Accurate assessment of glomerular filtration rate is central to renal evaluation in clinical and preclinical settings. Transcutaneous glomerular filtration rate offers practical advantages over conventionally measured glomerular filtration rate, including minimally invasive and continuous monitoring, but requires robust validation. The observations by Shimada et al. highlight both the promise and limitations of transcutaneous glomerular filtration rate, particularly in conditions that affect distribution volume, underscoring the need for rigorous evaluation across diverse physiological and disease states.

title: Gut-targeted interventions to complement PTH-lowering therapy
abstract: Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a major contributor to skeletal fragility in chronic kidney disease, yet fracture risk remains high despite parathyroid hormone-lowering therapy. In a rat model of chronic kidney disease, Allen et al. showed that combining the prebiotic fiber inulin with a calcimimetic further suppresses elevated bone turnover while improving cortical bone architecture and mechanical properties. These findings highlight the potential of gut-targeted interventions to complement established parathyroid hormone-lowering strategies for improving skeletal health.

Oxidative Stress Potentiates a STAT1–APOL1 Feedforward Loop and Governs Disease Severity in APOL1-Mediated Kidney Disease
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Apolipoprotein L1 (APOL1) risk variants (G1 and G2) confer immunity against Trypanosoma infection but markedly increase susceptibility to progressive kidney disease. However, only a subset of biallelic risk-variant carriers develops disease progression, distinct from murine models. Here, we evaluated molecular drivers of progressive kidney disease using a model that reflected the low human disease penetrance. METHODS: To investigate the heterogeneity of APOL1-mediated kidney disease, we generated novel APOL1 bacterial artificial chromosome transgenic mice with doxycycline-inducible systemic interferon-γ expression (G0- or G1-IFNγ mice). Podocyte-specific transcriptomics using translating ribosome affinity purification (TRAP-seq) and single-cell spatial transcriptomics via 10x Genomics Xenium In Situ platform was performed. Mechanistic validation and analysis of factors regulating APOL1 upregulation were conducted in primary podocytes and subsequently validated in mouse kidney and in human kidney biopsy specimens via immunofluorescence. RESULTS: A subset of G1-IFNγ mice developed severe albuminuria and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, which strongly correlated with the magnitude of APOL1 upregulation. By pairing TRAP-seq with single-cell spatial transcriptomic data, we identified mitochondrial dysfunction and JAK-STAT signaling as a central mediator of podocyte injury. In primary podocytes, APOL1 risk variants triggered mitochondrial-derived oxidative stress, establishing a self-amplifying STAT1-APOL1 feedforward loop that further enhances APOL1 expression and APOL1 oligomerization. This pathogenic loop was consistently enriched in podocytes from both G1-IFNγ mice and in kidney biopsy specimens from patients with APOL1-mediated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, demonstrating translational relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that biallelic risk variants initiate an oxidative stress-induced positive feedforward loop which promotes and sustains APOL1 upregulation and STAT1 phosphorylation, thereby contributing to disease susceptibility, severity and outcome.

title: Peritoneal dialysis induces hepatic metabolic stress as an instigator for systemic inflammation
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a lifesaving therapy in patients with kidney failure, but results in daily intraperitoneal glucose administration corresponding to 50% of the recommended energy intake, most of which enters the portal circulation. As the impact of this glucose exposure on liver and metabolic health remains unclear, we explored hepatic and systemic metabolic effects of PD. METHODS: Healthy mice and mice with chronic kidney disease (5/6 nephrectomy C57BL/6 aged 12-14 weeks) underwent seven weeks of PD. Combining morphologic studies, untargeted tissue proteomics, targeted plasma metabolomics and spatial transcriptomics, we assessed hepatic molecular and metabolic effects of PD. Gut- and gut-vascular barriers, systemic and hepatic lipopolysaccharide abundance and zonal transcriptional changes were assessed with multiplexed spatial single-cell analysis and transcriptomics. RESULTS: Intraperitoneally administered glucose during PD was rapidly taken up by the liver and induced hepatic metabolic inflammation. Portal-venous glucose overload bypassing the gastrointestinal tract resulted in increased glucose-to-cholesterol shunting with elevated plasma cholesterol levels, despite the absence of hepatic steatosis or glycogen storage. Increased oxidative stress and endotoxin load were associated with reduced hepatic Kupffer cell numbers without increased gut permeability. CONCLUSIONS: Ours study found chronic hepatic metabolic stress induced by PD. Evidence of hepatic glucotoxicity and oxidative stress as instigators for systemic metabolic inflammation induced by PD suggests that similar pathologic mechanisms could also contribute to increased cardiometabolic risk on chronic PD.

title: A study using the REIN registry suggests a statin therapy benefits for secondary prevention in patients receiving dialysis
abstract: INTRODUCTION: While statins are effective for cardiovascular prevention in the general population, their benefit in patients with CKD G5D (kidney failure treated by dialysis) remains uncertain. Previous randomized controlled trials included mixed populations for primary and secondary prevention while excluding patients with recent cardiovascular events, leaving a knowledge gap regarding statin effectiveness for secondary prevention immediately following an atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event. Here, we address this gap by providing real-world evidence. METHODS: We conducted a landmark-based observational study, informed by the target trial framework using the French Renal Epidemiology and Information Network (REIN) registry and merged with data from the French national healthcare system database from 2010 to 2023. We included adults with CKD G5D who experienced an ASCVD event. We used inverse probability of treatment weighting to balance baseline characteristics between statin initiators and non-initiators, thereby estimating the average causal effect on all-cause mortality. Results focus on the relative and absolute risk difference and the life expectancy gain using delta restricted mean survival time (dRMST). RESULTS: The study cohort included 5534 patients (median age: 75 years; 67% male). During the ten years of follow-up, statin use was associated with a reduced risk of mortality. The survival curves reached a maximum absolute difference at year four (risk difference -6.2% (95% CI: -10.2; -2.2); relative risk 0.88 [95% CI: 0.81; 0.96]). Life expectancy extended significantly over time with a mean survival gain of 69 days at five years (95% CI: 14-125) and reaching 135 days at ten years (95% CI: 31-239). No difference was identified between groups regarding hospitalizations for rhabdomyolysis or toxic hepatitis. CONCLUSIONS: In patients receiving dialysis, statin initiation following an ASCVD event is safe and associated with a modest-to-moderate ten-year cumulative survival benefit. While interpreted within observational limitations, this real-world evidence supports their use in this secondary prevention setting.

title: Safety outcomes of semaglutide by chronic kidney disease severity in the FLOW trial
abstract: Introduction People with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) often experience medication intolerance and side effects that worsen with lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This prespecified secondary analysis assessed the safety of semaglutide by baseline eGFR. Methods FLOW (NCT03819153) was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial testing the efficacy of subcutaneous semaglutide 1.0 mg once-weekly on a primary kidney outcome (50% or more eGFR reduction, kidney failure, or death due to kidney or cardiovascular causes) in participants with T2D and CKD. Safety data were collected selectively and included serious adverse events (SAEs), AEs leading to treatment discontinuation, and prespecified AEs of special interest (AESIs). In this descriptive assessment, systematically collected safety data were reported numerically by baseline eGFR. Results Of 3533 participants, 1767 received semaglutide and 1766 received placebo. Fewer SAEs were reported with semaglutide than placebo across baseline eGFR subgroups (45.1% versus 50.4% in the 60 or more ml/min per 1.73 m 2 subgroup, and 56.4% versus 60.4% in the under 30 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 subgroup). SAEs related to infections and infestations; cardiac disorders; respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorders; and metabolism and nutrition disorders were generally less frequent with semaglutide than placebo, regardless of baseline eGFR. Treatment discontinuations due to AEs were higher with lower baseline eGFR across treatment groups (60 or more ml/min per 1.73 m 2 : semaglutide 11.2%, placebo 11.3%; under30 ml/min per 66 1.73 m 2 : semaglutide 18.8%, placebo 18.7%). Discontinuations specifically due to gastrointestinal AEs were reported more frequently with semaglutide (4.5%) than placebo (1.1%), regardless of baseline eGFR. Frequencies of AESI were similar between treatment groups across baseline eGFR subgroups. Conclusions In this safety assessment, SAEs were reported less frequently with semaglutide than placebo, with corresponding patterns observed for treatment discontinuations and AESIs. No unexpected safety concerns were identified across the spectrum of eGFR represented in the FLOW trial.

title: The Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study measured hepcidin, cardiovascular, kidney and metabolic outcomes in chronic kidney disease
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Abnormal iron homeostasis plays a critical role in extra-hematopoietic disorders. The relationship of hepcidin, the master iron regulator, to clinical outcomes, has not been characterized in a large cohort of chronic kidney disease (CKD). METHODS: To determine if plasma hepcidin level predicts cardiovascular (CV), kidney, and metabolic outcomes in patients with CKD, we studied 3826 patients enrolled in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study. Hazard ratios for hepcidin tertiles were estimated from Cox Proportional Hazards regression for primary outcomes of incident heart failure (HF), end stage kidney disease (kidney failure) or halving of the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and new onset diabetes or prediabetes. Secondary outcomes included atherosclerotic events and all-cause and CV mortality. RESULTS: The median and interquartile range of plasma hepcidin level was 43 (22, 77) ng/mL. Higher plasma hepcidin levels were associated with older age, male sex, non-Hispanic Black race, diabetes, lower eGFR, higher albuminuria, increased plasma levels of iron indices, C-terminal fibroblast growth factor 23, and markers of inflammation (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and interleukin-6). We found no association between plasma hepcidin level and the risk for incident HF or prediabetes/diabetes. However, compared to the middle tertile, the highest hepcidin tertile was independently associated with increased risk for kidney outcomes (hazard ratio 1.19; 95% confidence interval 1.09, 1.30) and atherosclerotic events (hazard ratio 1.34; 95% confidence interval 1.09, 1.64), while the lowest hepcidin tertile was associated with increased risk for all-cause and CV mortality in fully adjusted multivariable models including iron indices and inflammation. CONCLUSION: Both low and high plasma levels of hepcidin are associated with adverse clinical outcomes.

title: Long-term efficacy and safety for the complement factor B inhibitor iptacopan in IgA nephropathy
abstract: Introduction Iptacopan, a factor B inhibitor, targets alternative complement pathway overactivation, a key driver of glomerular inflammation in IgA nephropathy. In the phase 3 APPLAUSE-IgAN trial (NCT04578834), iptacopan significantly slowed kidney function decline versus placebo over 24 months (difference in total estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] slope: 3.02 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 per year [95% confidence interval (CI) 2.02, 4.01; P < 0.001]). Methods Patients who completed APPLAUSE-IgAN or the phase 2 iptacopan trial (NCT03373461) could enter an open-label rollover extension program (REP) (NCT04557462). Patients in this REP receive oral iptacopan 200 mg twice daily alongside supportive care. Patients from the phase 2 trial were not included in efficacy analyses. Results Overall, 194 and 174 patients from the APPLAUSE-IgAN iptacopan and placebo arms, respectively, entered the REP. In patients who received iptacopan for up to 48 months, the total annualized eGFR slope was −3.49 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 per year (95% CI −4.17, −2.80). Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio from first morning void (UPCR-FMV) reduction was sustained through 48 months with iptacopan (geometric mean ratio to baseline: 0.61 [95% CI 0.50, 0.75]). Before receiving iptacopan, the total eGFR slope over 24 months in APPLAUSE-IgAN placebo arm patients who entered the REP was −5.29 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 per year (95% CI −6.09, −4.49). After switching to iptacopan, the total eGFR slope improved to −2.11 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 per year (95% CI −3.08, −1.13) over the next 24 months. UPCR-FMV decreased after switching (geometric mean ratio to baseline at month 48: 0.74 [95% CI 0.59, 0.91]). Long-term safety up to 5 years (median treatment duration: 29.9 months) was consistent with the known profile of iptacopan. Conclusions Long-term treatment with iptacopan led to sustained slowing in eGFR decline and proteinuria reduction that were also observed after switching from placebo. No new safety signals were observed. Trial Registration Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov with study numbers NCT04578834 (APPLAUSE-IgAN), NCT03373461 (phase 2 trial of iptacopan in IgAN), and NCT04557462 (rollover extension program).

title: Kidney International: 9 Years of Science, Community, and Change
abstract: At the end of 2026, a 9-year editorial cycle at Kidney International (KI) will come to a close, and a new chapter will begin. This transition offers an opportunity to reflect on how KI has evolved during a period of extraordinary change in nephrology and scientific publishing and, above all, what we have accomplished together—the editorial team, the contributors, and the readers of the journal.

title: Characterization of IgA, IgA immune complexes and complement depositions in IgA nephropathy using laser microdissection and mass spectrometry
abstract: Introduction IgA nephropathy is characterized by accumulation of mesangial IgA immune complexes. These IgA immune complexes result in glomerular inflammation and subsequent sclerosis. Glomerular inflammation is mediated in part by activation of the complement pathway by these immune complexes. Methods In this study of 22 cases of IgA nephropathy, using laser microdissection and mass spectrometry (LMD/MS), we characterized both IgA and complement deposits. Results LMD/MS detected abundant IgA1 but also IgA2; detected in 100% and 82% of cases, respectively. Furthermore, J chains, that link IgA monomers to form dimeric IgA on mucosal surfaces, was detected in 91% of cases, while the polymeric Ig receptor found in secretory IgA was found in only 9% of the cases. IgG1 was the dominant IgG subclass and was detected in 100% of cases. IgG subclass staining and confocal immunofluorescence microscopy confirmed the IgG1 subclass and colocalization of IgG1 with IgA1 and IgA2.Evaluation of the complement pathways revealed abundant C3, C9, C5, C6, C7 and C8 with lesser amounts of C4 indicating activation of predominantly the alternative and terminal pathways of complement. LMD/MS also detected abundant complement regulating proteins including CFH, CFHR1, CFHR2 and CFHR5, CD59, and smaller amounts of CFB, indicating active regulation of the complement pathways. Although it did not reach statistical significance, high counts of C3, C5 and C9 were present in lesions with endocapillary hypercellularity/crescentic lesions. High counts of complement regulating proteins, particularly CFHR5, were also present in active lesions. C3 sequence coverage data showed the majority of amino acids detected belong to C3dg along with smaller amounts of C3c. Conclusion Our data shows that the IgA immune complexes are composed of mucosal-derived dimeric IgA1/IgA2 and IgG1. The majority of complement proteins detected are components of the alternative and terminal complement pathway.

title: Alloimmune risk stratification for kidney transplantation
abstract: Alloreactivity after kidney transplantation occurs via both memory responses resulting from prior sensitization and de novo responses that develop due to donor-recipient disparity for the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) complex. HLA compatibility (absence of HLA-DSA) and the degree of HLA matching inform on the likelihood of allorecognition that can cause allograft rejection and allograft loss, and are therefore the two pillars of alloimmune risk assessment. Over the past decades, the detection of anti-HLA antibodies has become more sensitive and specific through single antigen bead testing, and advances in HLA typing from serology to DNA level have been instrumental for more detailed analysis of HLA compatibility. Nonetheless, alloimmune risk stratification using antigen-level HLA data has limited ability to accurately predict the risk of de novo anti-HLA responses and long-term graft outcome after transplantation, especially on the individual patient level. Aiming to improve long-term outcomes by improving HLA matching, HLA molecular mismatch algorithms have been developed. In this review, we discuss the advances, clinical evidence, limitations and clinical implementability of HLA molecular mismatch analysis to increase precision in alloimmune risk stratification in kidney transplantation. In addition, we provide an overview of the different molecular mismatch tools and their potential application in personalized medicine, such as organ allocation, criteria for donor acceptance and individualized immunosuppression.

title: Kidney Endpoints in ANCA-Associated Vasculitis – Position Report from the European Vasculitis Society Focus Group Meetings
abstract: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitides (AAV) often affect the kidneys, driving morbidity and mortality in AAV. Clinical trials have investigated kidney outcomes using a variety of definitions. The standardization of kidney disease response criteria in AAV remains an unmet need, with an urgency to define kidney endpoints for daily clinical practice and new drug development to optimize patient management. A European Vasculitis Society (EUVAS) Focus Group was formed to review the literature and discuss the wide range of definitions used. The group involved nephrologists, pathologists and rheumatologists who met four times over a time frame of two years with the objective of formulating a consensus proposal for standardized kidney endpoint definitions for AAV. The group investigated the terminology and outcome relations of active kidney disease, treatment response and refractory kidney disease, remission and relapse, kidney function recovery and kidney failure requiring kidney replacement therapy. The group reviewed and discussed measurable parameters used for the assessments, such as kidney biopsy, hematuria and proteinuria, serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate and novel biomarkers. Here, we report on the current variability in terminology, present an expert proposal for kidney endpoints with a research agenda and outline the future strategy for a Delphi consensus.
